name: King Oak

location.address: Charleville Forest, Charleville Demesne, Tullamore, County Offaly, Ireland

access: Free. The tree stands just inside the main entrance to Charleville Forest demesne, whose woodland walks are open to the public year-round with no entrance fee; the castle itself is a separate paid/booked tour and not needed to reach the tree.
transport: Roughly 3 km / 40 minute walk from Tullamore town centre; no rail station in Tullamore serves the estate directly, but Tullamore has an Irish Rail station on the Dublin-Galway line.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree closely: contest page gives 400-800 years and branches reaching ~27m (contest text mistranslated as 50m via a search summary, discard that figure, use Wikipedia's 27m which matches the contest's own 'touch the ground' framing); Wikipedia gives girth 8.29m (829cm), height 19m, branch spread up to 27m, and independently corroborates the 400-800 year range and the 17th-century first mention. Heavily pollarded historically for timber; lower branches are propped to prevent falling, which is itself part of the visitor experience (a tree visibly held up). Story hook: local superstition holds that a falling branch predicts the death of a member of the Bury family who have owned the estate; in 1963 lightning split the main trunk and Charles Howard-Bury died weeks later, which locals point to as confirmation. Also a generational rite: local teenagers reportedly climbed it as a test of courage. Featured in Thomas Pakenham's 'Meetings with Remarkable Trees'. Finished 3rd in European Tree of the Year 2013 with 5,785 votes. Would somebody travel specifically for this one tree: yes, it is Ireland's best-known single tree and the estate's own 'star attraction' per Wikipedia, standing alone with no other known remarkable trees nearby (67km to nearest published tree, Dublin).

name: Niel Gow's Oak

location.address: Inver Walk, Craigvinean Forest, south bank of the River Tay, near Dunkeld, Perth and Kinross, Scotland

access: Free. Stands beside the Inver Walk, part of the public Dunkeld Path Network, on Forestry Commission (now Forestry and Land Scotland) land; a bench and plaque sit at the tree.
transport: About 1.5 km / 20 minute walk from Dunkeld along the Tay-side path from Inver village; Dunkeld & Birnam has a mainline railway station roughly 2 km away.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree: contest page and Wikipedia both give roughly 300 years (seeded circa 1700), Wikipedia gives exact coordinates on the Inver Walk footpath, Woodland Trust's Ancient Tree Inventory (a public register, a third corroborating source) gives girth 5.90m measured at 1.5m height (590cm) and notes hollowing trunk and branches with decaying wood in the crown, consistent with the age. Story hook: linked since at least 1855 (Illustrated London News) to Niel Gow (1727-1807), the most celebrated Scottish fiddler of his day, who lived in nearby Inver; local tradition holds he composed many of his best-loved tunes sitting beneath this oak, with the sound said to have carried across the river to the Duke of Atholl. A bench beside the tree carries lyrics from Michael Marra's song 'Niel Gow's Apprentice'; the original bench was destroyed by falling branches in December 2012 and replaced March 2013, showing the tree is actively maintained and visited. First Scottish entry in European Tree of the Year, placing 7th of 10 in 2014 with 1,740 votes; also shortlisted for Scotland's Tree of the Year 2016. Would somebody travel specifically for this one tree: yes, it is a named stop on the Dunkeld path network with its own bench, plaque and folklore, standing alone with no other known remarkable trees nearby (28km to nearest published tree, the Fortingall Yew).

name: The Oak at the Gate of the Dead

location.address: B4500 roadside, Ceiriog Valley, near Chirk Castle, Wrexham County Borough, Wales

access: Free. Stands directly beside the B4500 public road about 300m from Chirk Castle, and on the route of the Offa's Dyke Path (a National Trail); no permission needed, visible and reachable from the roadside verge.
transport: About 300m walk from Chirk Castle car park; Chirk railway station (Wrexham-Shrewsbury line) is roughly 3km away.
verify_notes: Two independent sources plus a third (Woodland Trust's Ancient Tree Forum/Inventory): estimated over 1000 years old, possibly seeded during the reign of King Ecgberht (802-839). Coordinates from the contest and Wikipedia match almost exactly, confirming the pin. Girth was historically about 10m but the trunk split into two during cold weather in February 2010; Wrexham County Borough Council placed a tree preservation order on it afterward, and a 2022 measurement (Woodland Trust ATI, dated 26 January 2022) gives a narrowest girth of 7.52m (752cm) at 1.4-1.6m, which is the current, post-split figure and the one recorded here; note the pre-2010 10m figure in case the writer wants the 'before and after' as a story beat. Alive and recently measured (2022), so confirmation is recent and solid despite the historic damage. Story hook: named for the 1165 Battle of Crogen, when a Welsh army under Owain Gwynedd ambushed and defeated an invading English army under Henry II near this spot, with the dead said to be buried nearby (the valley's old name, Adwy'r Beddau, means 'pass of the graves'). Identified and named by Woodland Trust recorder Rob McBride in 2007; a plaque was unveiled in March 2009. First Welsh nomination for European Tree of the Year, finishing 9th of 10 in 2014 with 1,093 votes; has its own long-running Facebook page and TV appearances per the contest text. Would somebody travel specifically for this one tree: yes, a named, plaqued, roadside veteran with a documented battle legend and a visible survival story (split in half and still standing), 48km from the nearest published tree.

name: Waverley Abbey Yew

location.address: Waverley Abbey ruins, off B3001 near Tilford, Farnham, Surrey, England

access: Free. English Heritage manages Waverley Abbey and admits visitors at any reasonable time during daylight hours, no entrance fee. A roughly 350m walk across a field (uneven ground, a kissing gate, and grazing cattle) leads to the ruins where the yew stands; small on-site car park.
transport: About a 5 minute walk from the on-site car park; Farnham railway station is roughly 3km away, with the abbey otherwise reached by car or bus plus a short walk.
verify_notes: Two independent sources: contest page gives roughly 500 years and multi-stemmed growth over the abbey ruins; Woodland Trust's Ancient Tree Inventory gives girth 6.78m at 1.30m height (678cm). Its true age is genuinely uncertain rather than firmly dated: most sources say it took root sometime after the Dissolution of the Monasteries in 1536, so 'over 500 years' is itself already close to the outer bound of what is documented, and the tree may be younger than it looks, which is worth stating plainly rather than smoothing over. Story hook: rooted directly among the ruins of a 12th-century Cistercian abbey (founded 1128, dissolved 1536), multi-stemmed with roots that arch above ground before diving back in, and holes and decay in the trunk that make it a wildlife habitat. Won the Woodland Trust's UK Tree of the Year 2022 before going on to the European contest in 2023, where it placed 7th of 10 with 9,413 votes. Would somebody travel specifically for this one tree: yes, a UK Tree of the Year winner standing inside a free, open, English Heritage ruin with its own visible drama (growing out of monastic stonework), 23km from the nearest published tree.

name: The Acton Park Sweet Chestnut
access: Free. Acton Park is an ordinary public park run by Wrexham Council, on the edge of the city centre, open at all normal park hours with no entrance fee.
transport: Acton Park sits within Wrexham city, roughly a 25 minute walk from Wrexham Central railway station.
verify_notes: Two independent local sources plus the contest page. Age is given inconsistently: the contest text says '500+ years', while Wrexham.com and Forestry Journal both say approximately 480-484 years (planted around 1534-1546, during the reign of Henry VIII, not Elizabeth I as one search summary garbled; discard that). Recording the range rather than picking a winner. Girth 6.1m (610cm), height 24m, both from Wrexham.com citing the council's own figures. No tree-level coordinates were found beyond the contest's park-level GPS pin (which sits inside the park boundary but is not confirmed against a specific trunk), so location_precision is approximate; a later pass or reader correction could tighten this to the actual tree location within the park. Story hook: survived the park being 'plundered for firewood' in the hardship of the 1940s postwar years, and has come through 'dozens of deadly storms' including the severe storms of 2021 that toppled or maimed neighbouring trees; today it is 'the centrepiece of picnics and tree parties' for locals, i.e. an actively used community gathering tree rather than a roped-off relic. Won the UK's Woodland Trust Tree of the Year 2023 with 17% of the vote (Wrexham Council and Coed Cadw nominated it) before placing 10th of 10 in the European contest 2024 with 7,180 votes. Would somebody travel specifically for this one tree: plausible but weaker than the others here, since it is a fine but ordinary-looking park chestnut whose case rests on being a reigning UK Tree of the Year winner rather than on visible spectacle; 36km from the nearest published tree (Liverpool).

name: The Skipinnish Oak

location.address: Sitka spruce plantation, Achnacarry Estate, near Loch Arkaig, Lochaber, Scottish Highlands

access: Free, but not a park: the tree stands within a working Sitka spruce plantation on the privately owned Achnacarry Estate. Woodland Trust's Ancient Tree Inventory records its access category as 'Public - Scottish Outdoor Access', i.e. covered by Scotland's statutory right of responsible access (the Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003 / Scottish Outdoor Access Code) rather than by an estate invitation; there is no visitor infrastructure, marked path or car park, and forestry operations (harvesting machinery, felled timber) may be present. Say plainly on the page that this is a bushwhack into a commercial plantation, not a stroll.
transport: No public transport reaches Achnacarry directly; nearest railway station is Spean Bridge (West Highland Line), a few km away, then a walk/drive along the Great Glen to the estate and into the plantation. No official visitor route exists, so give the honest caveat that reaching the exact tree requires local knowledge or a GPS device.
verify_notes: Three independent sources beyond the contest page: Wikipedia, the Woodland Trust's own Ancient Tree Inventory (register entry, treeId 236486, recorded 10/11/2022, last visited 29/10/2024) and the Trust's press release. Species disagreement worth flagging: the contest page calls it 'Common Oak (Quercus robur)' while both Wikipedia and the ATI register call it Sessile Oak (Quercus petraea); the register identification is the more authoritative and is used here, but note the discrepancy for the writer. Girth from the ATI register: 8.00m at 1.50m height (800cm), among the largest of these eight candidates. Coordinate discrepancy: the contest's published GPS and Wikipedia's stated coordinates differ by roughly 1-2km (the ATI's own grid reference, NN1836086242, was not converted precisely here), consistent with this being a tree found by chance in trackless plantation rather than a signposted landmark; location_precision is therefore approximate rather than confirmed, honestly. Age is stated as 'at least 400 years' by the contest and Wikipedia; one secondary article speculates it could be up to 1,000, which is unsourced beyond that article and should not be repeated as fact. Story hook: unknown to foresters until 2009, when members of the Scottish ceilidh band Skipinnish, performing nearby for a Native Woodland Discussion Group event, mentioned the tree (one band member's father had told him about it) and led experts to it the next day, which is how it reached the Ancient Tree Inventory and got its name; also carries the rare 'black-eyed Susan' lichen (Heterodermia leucomelos), seldom found outside western Scotland, plus cuckoo epiphytes and beefsteak fungus per the register. Designated a Scottish 'Heritage Tree' and a 'Tree of National Special Interest'. Won UK Tree of the Year 2024 (21% of the public vote among a shortlist of 12), then competed in the European contest, placing 7th (UK winner) in 2025 with 16,771 votes. Would somebody travel specifically for this one tree: plausible on fame (a reigning UK Tree of the Year winner with a good discovery story) but the access and pin are both genuinely rough; flag this one for Hidde's eyes given the working-forestry setting and the coordinate uncertainty, rather than treating it as settled. 69km from the nearest published tree (the Fortingall Yew).
